opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the conventional application is close to the least informative signal they get. What people at the labs are really looking for is evidence that you can do the work, and that you'll do it whether or not anyone tells you to.

The single strongest signal is having done something real on your own initiative. That might be a blog post where you went deep on a technical question, reproduced a paper, and found something surprising. It might be an open-source contribution, or a small research project where you clearly pushed past the point where most people would have stopped. When someone at a lab reads that and thinks "this person is already doing the job," that beats almost any credential.

The second thing is agency. The field moves so fast that nobody can hand you a well-specified task and a clear path. People want to know if you'll take a fuzzy problem, figure out what actually matters, and drive it to completion. Lots of people are smart. Far fewer will grind through the unglamorous parts like debugging infrastructure, staring at loss curves, or rewriting the data pipeline because it's the thing blocking progress.

Third is taste: knowing which problems are worth working on and which experiments will actually tell you something. That's hard to show on a CV but very visible in how someone writes about their work.

So my advice is usually to stop optimizing the application and make your work public. Put it somewhere people can see it. A lot of hiring in this field happens because someone noticed you, not because you went through a portal. If you do genuinely good work in the open, the right people tend to find it surprisingly quickly.

r001.rationale: The response says the strongest signal is having done something real on your own initiative and describes pursuing projects independently.

r002.rationale: It says employers want evidence you can do the work, but does not state that they seek world-class ability at a particular task.

r003.rationale: It gives examples such as a technical blog post or research project, but does not describe creating a definitive reference for a problem that lacked adequate coverage.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the conventional application tells you almost nothing about the things that actually matter in this field. A résumé tells you where someone has been, not what they can do when nobody's handed them a well-defined problem.

What I've seen work, and what I think most labs are implicitly selecting for, is some evidence that you've done the thing already. Not a course, not a certificate, but something you built or figured out on your own because you were genuinely curious. Someone who reimplemented a paper, found it didn't replicate, and then spent two weeks working out why. Someone who wrote up a weird result on their blog and was wrong about half of it but right about the half that mattered. That kind of artifact is incredibly legible. It shows you can pick a direction, sustain effort without external validation, and be honest about what you found.

The second thing is agency, which sounds like a buzzword but is very concrete in practice. Research moves fast enough now that nobody can tell you exactly what to do. If you need the problem fully specified before you start, you'll be perpetually behind. The people who are most valuable are the ones who notice something is off, go investigate it, and come back with an answer before anyone asked the question. You can often see this in how someone describes their past work. Do they talk about what they were assigned, or about what they chose and why?

Third, and this is underrated, is taste. There are a thousand things you could try, and most of them are a waste of time. Knowing which experiments are actually informative, which ones are likely to just confirm what you already believe, which ones are the cheap tests of the expensive hypothesis. That's hard to teach and very hard to fake in a conversation. When I talk to someone, I'm often trying to figure out whether they have a model of why things work, not just that they do.

And then there's the boring stuff that turns out to be load-bearing. Can you write clearly? Can you debug something for six hours without losing your mind? Do you actually read the code, or just the abstract? Those matter more than people expect, because so much of the real work is unglamorous.

So if someone asked me how to stand out, I'd say: stop optimizing the application and go do something real that you can point to. The application is just a pointer. The thing it points to is what gets you hired.

r001.rationale: The response says employers value work someone pursued independently out of curiosity and describes agency in identifying and investigating problems without being told.

r002.rationale: It discusses evidence of ability and strong research judgment, but does not say employers seek world-class performance at a particular task.

r003.rationale: It recommends building or investigating something real, but does not describe creating a definitive technical reference for an inadequately covered problem.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re looking for evidence that you can take an ambiguous problem and actually make progress on it. A conventional application tells you where somebody went to university and which jobs they’ve had. It doesn’t necessarily tell you what happens when you give them something nobody knows how to do yet.

So one of the most useful things you can do is build something or investigate a question you’re genuinely curious about. It doesn’t have to be some enormous project. You could reproduce a paper, notice that one of the results is strange, and dig into why. If you can explain what you tried, what failed, and what you learned, that gives someone a much richer signal than a list of qualifications.

And there’s a difference between saying, “I’m really interested in AI,” and having followed that interest far enough that you have your own questions. Those questions give you something substantive to talk about with the people you want to work with. You’re already doing a small version of the work.

r001.rationale: It says employers value evidence you can independently take an ambiguous problem and make progress, and recommends pursuing a project or question from genuine curiosity.

r002.rationale: The response describes making progress on an ambiguous problem but does not say employers seek proof of world-class performance at a particular task.

r003.rationale: It recommends building something or investigating a question, but does not present creating a definitive technical reference for an inadequately covered problem as a way to attract employers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re looking for evidence that you can do the work, and that you’re unusually motivated to do it. A conventional application tells you where someone went to university and what jobs they’ve had. It doesn’t necessarily tell you what happens when you give them an ambiguous problem and say, “Go figure this out.”

So if you’ve reproduced a paper, built something useful, or investigated a question and written up what you found, that gives people something much more concrete to evaluate. It doesn’t have to be a huge project. A small, thoughtful piece of work where you can explain your decisions and what surprised you can be a very strong signal.

And there’s an element of initiative: did you need someone to hand you a well-defined task, or did you notice something worth doing and actually do it?

r001.rationale: The response says employers look for initiative, including noticing something worth doing and doing it without being handed a defined task.

r002.rationale: It says employers want evidence that someone can do the work, but does not claim world-class ability at a particular task.

r003.rationale: It mentions projects and write-ups as evidence, but not creating a definitive technical reference for an inadequately covered problem.
